title: Why Honeybees Dance
paras: When a honeybee finds a good source of flowers, it returns to the hive and performs a short dance.
The dance tells the other bees where to find the food.
Scientists first described this behavior in the 1940s, and their discovery later won a Nobel Prize.
Before then, most people believed that insects could not share such detailed information.
There are two main types of dance.
If the food is close to the hive, the bee makes a circle.
The circle shows that flowers are nearby, but it does not point in any particular direction.
If the food is far away, the bee performs a figure-eight dance known as the waggle dance.
During the straight middle part, the bee shakes its body quickly from side to side.
The waggle dance contains two kinds of information.
The angle of the straight part, measured against the vertical wall of the hive, shows the direction of the flowers compared with the sun.
The length of the waggle shows the distance, so a longer waggle means that the flowers are farther away.
Other bees follow the dancer closely and then fly out to look for the flowers themselves.

insert.sentence: Which one a bee performs depends on how far away the flowers are.

title: How Glaciers Move
paras: A glacier is a huge mass of ice that forms over many years in places where snow does not melt completely in summer.
Each year, new snow falls on top of the old snow and presses it down.
Slowly, the lower layers turn into dense ice.
When the ice becomes thick enough, it begins to move.
Glaciers move in two main ways.
First, the ice itself can bend and flow very slowly, like thick honey, under the weight above it.
Second, a glacier can slide along the ground when a thin layer of water forms at its base.
This water may come from melting caused by pressure or by heat from the ground, and it works like oil between two surfaces.
Because of these two processes, some glaciers move only a few centimeters a day, while fast ones may travel dozens of meters.
As glaciers move, they change the land around them.
They carry rocks and gravel that scrape the ground like sandpaper.
Over thousands of years, this action can turn a narrow river valley into a wide U-shaped valley.
When a glacier finally melts, it leaves behind piles of rock that it carried, which show scientists where the ice once reached.

title: Waiting for Two Marshmallows
paras: In the late 1960s, the psychologist Walter Mischel tested a simple idea with preschool children at Stanford University.
A researcher placed one marshmallow in front of each child and offered a deal.
If the child could wait alone for about fifteen minutes without eating it, he or she would receive a second marshmallow.
Some children ate the treat almost immediately, while others found clever ways to distract themselves.
Years later, Mischel and his colleagues followed up with many of the participants.
They reported that children who had waited longer tended to have higher test scores and better social skills as teenagers.
The results spread quickly, and the study became a popular symbol of self-control.
Many parents and teachers concluded that the ability to delay gratification is a key to success.
More recent research has questioned this conclusion.
In 2018, a team of researchers repeated the experiment with a much larger and more diverse group of children.
They found that the link between waiting time and later achievement was considerably weaker than the original studies suggested.
Once the researchers accounted for the children's family background, such as parents' education and income, the connection almost disappeared.
This suggests that a child's willingness to wait may reflect how reliable the child's environment is, not just self-control alone.

insert.sentence: However, the original group was small, and most of the children came from families connected with the university.

qs.stem: What can be inferred about the original Stanford studies from paragraph 3?
opts: Their results may not have applied to all kinds of children.
They included more children than later research.

qs.ex: Повторное исследование использовало «much larger and more diverse group» — значит, исходная группа была меньше и менее разнообразной. Отсюда осторожность в обобщениях.

qs.ex: Вставка с «However» критикует вывод, сделанный в конце абзаца, и подводит к следующему абзацу («More recent research has questioned this conclusion»). Раньше она разорвала бы описание популярности результата.

title: Moving Type in Korea
paras: Many people associate the invention of movable type with Johannes Gutenberg, who printed books in Germany around 1450.
However, printers in Korea had been using metal type for more than two centuries before that.
The oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type is a Korean Buddhist text called the Jikji, produced in 1377.
Its pages were printed from small metal pieces, each carrying a single Chinese character.
Despite this early start, movable type did not transform Korean society the way it later changed Europe.
One reason was the writing system itself.
Classical texts used thousands of different Chinese characters.
A European printer, by contrast, needed only a few dozen letters, which could be combined to make any word.
Another reason was that printing in Korea was controlled mostly by the government and by temples, which printed small numbers of books for officials and monks.
Gutenberg's workshop operated in a very different setting.
He sold books to a growing group of merchants, students, and church leaders who wanted to buy them.
As demand rose, printers across Europe competed to produce books quickly and cheaply, which spread the technology even further.
In this way, the commercial setting mattered at least as much as the invention itself.

insert.sentence: As a result, a printer had to make and store an enormous number of metal pieces.

title: The Box That Changed Shipping
paras: Until the 1950s, loading a cargo ship was slow, expensive work.
Goods arrived at the port in barrels, sacks, and wooden crates of every shape and size.
Teams of dockworkers carried each item on board by hand or with simple cranes, and a ship might wait in port for a week or more.
Because loading took so long, ships earned money for only part of the year, and the cost of shipping a product was often higher than the cost of making it.
In 1956, an American trucking businessman named Malcolm McLean tried a different approach.
He had large steel boxes of one standard shape lifted directly from trucks onto a ship, without opening them.
The cargo stayed sealed inside the container until it reached its destination.
Loading times fell from days to hours, and goods were damaged and stolen far less often.
Containers soon changed the global economy.
Once other shippers agreed on standard sizes, a container could move easily from a ship to a train or truck.
Ports invested in huge cranes and large storage areas, and many older ports that could not adapt lost business.
As shipping became cheaper, it made sense for companies to manufacture goods in distant countries and sell them everywhere.

insert.sentence: They could also be stacked several layers high, which made better use of space on the ship.

title: Why the Night Sky Is Dark
paras: At first glance, the darkness of the night sky seems too obvious to need an explanation.
Yet in the nineteenth century, the German astronomer Heinrich Olbers pointed out a puzzle.
If the universe were infinite and filled evenly with stars that have existed forever, every line of sight from Earth would eventually end on the surface of a star.
The entire sky would therefore blaze as brightly as the surface of the Sun, even at midnight.
Astronomers eventually realized that the puzzle disappears once we accept that the universe has a history.
Light travels at a finite speed, so we can only see objects whose light has had enough time to reach us.
Because the universe is about 13.8 billion years old, light from beyond a certain distance has not yet arrived.
The number of stars that can contribute light to our night sky is therefore limited.
A second factor is that the universe is expanding.
As distant galaxies move away from us, the light they emit is stretched to longer wavelengths, shifting from visible light toward infrared and microwaves.
Much of this energy is no longer visible to the human eye, even though it still reaches us.
In fact, it forms a faint glow of microwaves detected in every direction, which scientists regard as a remnant of the early universe.

insert.sentence: Beyond that distance, the universe may contain countless stars that we cannot see.

It was solved by Olbers himself.
It showed that stars do not produce light.

qs.ex: Загадка строится на условии «если Вселенная бесконечна и вечна». Второй абзац показывает, что Вселенная имеет историю, — значит, исходные допущения были неверны.

title: Paint in a Tube
paras: Before the middle of the nineteenth century, painters who wanted to work outdoors faced a practical problem.
Oil paint was sold in animal bladders tied with string, and it dried out or spilled when carried from one place to another.
As a result, most artists painted indoors, working from sketches made outside.
Landscapes created in the studio often looked formal and carefully arranged rather than fresh.
In 1841, the American portrait painter John Goffe Rand patented a collapsible metal tube with a screw cap.
Paint could now be stored for months, squeezed out in small amounts, and sealed again.
The invention was inexpensive to manufacture, and manufacturers soon began filling tubes with a wide range of ready-made colors.
Artists no longer needed to grind pigments by hand with assistants, which had previously required a workshop.
The result was a new way of painting.
Claude Monet and Pierre-Auguste Renoir carried portable easels into fields and gardens and painted directly from what they saw.
They worked quickly to capture changing light, using short, visible brushstrokes instead of smooth, hidden ones.
Renoir is said to have remarked that without paint in tubes there would have been no Impressionism.

To show that painters preferred natural materials
To describe how colors were mixed

title: The Commons Revisited
paras: In 1968, the ecologist Garrett Hardin described a problem that he called the tragedy of the commons.
He asked readers to imagine a pasture open to all the herders in a village.
Each herder gains personally from adding one more animal, but the cost of overgrazing is shared by everyone.
Because every herder reasons in the same way, the pasture is eventually destroyed.
Hardin concluded that shared resources inevitably collapse unless they are privatized or controlled by a government.
His argument was widely applied to fisheries, forests, and the atmosphere.
Yet the political scientist Elinor Ostrom, who studied communities around the world, found many cases that did not fit his prediction.
Mountain villages in Switzerland, for example, have managed shared pastures for centuries.
According to Ostrom, successful communities share certain features.
Members clearly know who is allowed to use the resource, and they create rules that suit local conditions.
Those who break the rules are monitored and receive penalties that start small and increase for repeated violations.
Ostrom received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2009 for showing that people can often solve such problems without relying on either markets or central authorities.

insert.sentence: Every herder therefore has a reason to add more animals.

qs.stem: What can be inferred about Hardin's argument from paragraph 2?
opts: It overlooked communities that managed shared resources successfully.
It was proven correct by Ostrom's research.
It was ignored by policy makers.
It applied only to pastures.
qs.ex: Остром нашла «many cases that did not fit his prediction» — значит, аргумент Хардина не учитывал успешные общины. Он применялся и к рыболовству, лесам, атмосфере.

qs.ex: «therefore» требует причины перед собой (выгода каждого пастуха), а следующее предложение («reasons in the same way») ссылается на это рассуждение. Поэтому вставка идёт после третьего предложения.

qs.ex: Суть: премия за доказательство, что люди часто решают такие проблемы без рынка и центральной власти. Остальные варианты искажают причину награды.

title: Underground Partners
paras: Beneath a forest floor lies a vast network of fine fungal threads that connect to the roots of nearly all plants.
This partnership, known as a mycorrhiza, benefits both sides.
The fungus extends the plant's reach into the soil, absorbing water and minerals such as phosphorus that roots could not easily gather alone.
In exchange, the plant supplies the fungus with sugars produced through photosynthesis.
Some researchers have proposed that these fungal threads also link trees to one another, forming what has been called a wood-wide web.
In laboratory experiments, carbon atoms taken up by one tree have later been detected in neighboring trees.
Supporters suggest that older, larger trees might use the network to send resources to shaded seedlings, improving the young trees' chance of survival.
Such interpretations have attracted enormous public interest.
Other scientists urge caution.
They point out that evidence of carbon moving between plants does not show that the transfer is intended to help the recipient or that it makes a significant difference in a natural forest.
The fungus itself might retain much of the carbon, and seedlings may survive mainly because of the light and water around them.
Most researchers agree that the networks exist, but how much they shape forest life remains an open question.

insert.sentence: These results suggested that trees might exchange resources through the fungi.

qs.stem: The word "retain" in the passage is closest in meaning to
opts: keep
produce

title: Cards and Looms
paras: The origins of modern computing are often traced to machines for arithmetic, but another source was weaving.
In 1804, the French inventor Joseph-Marie Jacquard demonstrated a loom that could weave complicated patterns automatically.
Instead of relying on a skilled worker to choose each thread, the loom read instructions from a chain of cards with holes punched in them.
Where a hole appeared, a hook could pass through and lift a thread; where there was none, the thread stayed down.
Because the pattern was stored on cards rather than in a person's memory, it could be changed by replacing the cards.
A weaver could also produce exactly the same design again whenever it was needed.
Some workers feared that the machine would take their jobs, and a few attacked such looms, but the technology spread throughout Europe.
By the middle of the century, tens of thousands of Jacquard looms were in use.
The idea also attracted the English mathematician Charles Babbage.
In the 1830s he designed the Analytical Engine, a mechanical calculator that was to be controlled by punched cards.
His collaborator Ada Lovelace recognized that such a machine could manipulate not only numbers but any symbols that followed rules, such as music.
Although the machine was never completed, later inventors used punched cards to store data, and they remained in use for computers well into the twentieth century.

title: The Year Without a Summer
paras: In April 1815, the volcano Mount Tambora, on an island in present-day Indonesia, erupted with enormous force.
It threw more than one hundred cubic kilometers of ash and rock into the air, making it the largest eruption in recorded history.
The explosion and its immediate effects killed tens of thousands of people nearby.
However, the most widespread consequences were felt thousands of kilometers away, and they appeared a year later.
The eruption released large quantities of sulfur gas into the stratosphere, where it combined with water to form tiny droplets.
These droplets reflected some sunlight back into space, reducing the energy that reached the surface of the Earth.
As a result, average temperatures in parts of the Northern Hemisphere fell by as much as one degree Celsius in 1816, which was enough to disrupt the growing season.
Spring frosts were followed by cold, rainy summers, and snow was reported in New England in June.
Harvests failed across Europe and North America, and food prices rose steeply.
In many regions, farmers faced hunger and some families left their homes to search for food or to start new lives elsewhere.
The gloomy weather also left a mark on culture.
Confined indoors during a stormy summer in Switzerland, the young writer Mary Shelley began the story that became Frankenstein.

insert.sentence: Rain does not reach this layer, so the droplets stay aloft for a long time.

title: When a New Road Makes Traffic Worse
paras: Common sense suggests that adding a new road to a congested network should make travel faster.
In 1968, however, the mathematician Dietrich Braess showed that this is not always true.
Under certain conditions, a new road can increase the travel time for every driver in the network.
The result seems paradoxical, but it follows from a simple feature of how people choose their routes.
Imagine two routes between a suburb and a city center, each with one slow but steady stretch and one fast stretch that becomes crowded when many cars use it.
Drivers divide themselves roughly evenly between the two routes, and each trip takes a similar amount of time.
Now suppose a short connecting road is built that lets drivers combine the two fast stretches.
Each driver, looking only at his or her own journey, finds the new shortcut attractive.
As more drivers switch, the fast stretches become congested, and everyone ends up with a longer trip than before.
Researchers think that similar effects occasionally occur in real cities.
In 2005, Seoul removed an elevated highway through the city center and replaced it with a stream and park, yet traffic in the area did not collapse as many had feared.
Transportation planners are cautious about drawing general conclusions from such cases.
Nevertheless, the idea reminds them that individual choices can produce results that nobody wants.

insert.sentence: In other words, everyone would be better off if the shortcut did not exist.
